text: A guest book that knows who is coming. The lantern is lit.
picture: The Storyteller stands in a dark, misty hollow, his face solemn and knowing. He holds a glowing red lantern low at his side, casting a warm circle of light on the mist swirling at his boots. Far behind him, the faint dark outline of a lonely roadside motel is barely visible in the dense fog, with a single window glowing faintly.

text: I work the night desk at the Wayside Motel, out on Route 9, where the road runs between two towns that don't talk to each other.
picture: A long, wide shot of the Wayside Motel at night. It's a single-storey, run-down building with a row of identical, dark doors, standing alone by an empty two-lane road. A single window at the front office glows with dim yellow light. There are no cars or people anywhere, and a low fog blankets the ground. No signs are visible.

text: Twelve rooms. Most nights, nobody comes.
picture: A close-up on an old leather-bound guest book lying open on a worn wooden desk counter. The pages are covered in faint, faded handwriting. A brass desk bell and a single desk lamp sit nearby. The lamplight falls across the page, its columns too small to read clearly.

text: The guest book sits open on the counter. The owner, Mr. Pell, likes ink. He says a name in ink is a promise.
picture: June stands behind the wooden counter in grey dawn light filtering through a window, looking tired. Mr. Pell stands just beside the counter, looking down at the book. His hands rest on the counter, one finger pointing gently at the open page.

text: Every morning, when I hand over the keys, there's a new line in it. Room six. Signed at two fourteen a.m. A different name every night.
picture: June now stands close to the counter in the grey dawn light, looking troubled. One of her hands holds a simple ring of old motel keys. Her other hand rests on the open guest book, her index finger pointing under a single line written in fresh, vivid blood-red ink that stands out starkly against the pale yellowed page. The writing itself is an unreadable blur.

text: Room six has been boarded up since before I was hired.
picture: An exterior night shot focused on one motel door. The brass number 6 hangs crookedly on weathered wood. The door is completely boarded shut with old, grey, splintered planks. A single dim yellow bulb overhead casts harsh shadows from the nails and boards. Thick fog presses in close around the doorframe, obscuring everything else.

text: The first week, I blamed the day staff. The second week, I stopped blaming anyone. I started watching.
picture: June sits rigid at the front desk, both hands clutching her phone. The open guest book lies before her, its red ink hidden. Blackness fills the window behind her. Her face is pale, alert, and hollow with fatigue.

text: Last night, at two thirteen, the lights in the parking lot flickered.
picture: An exterior shot from the office window. In the dark parking lot, the tall sodium light poles strobe and gutter, throwing sickly orange pulses across the empty asphalt and the motel doors.

text: At two fourteen, the pen moved.
picture: An extreme close insert on the surface of the guest book. A dark wood fountain pen lies at a slight, unnatural angle, as if nudged. The desk lamp light is dim and unsteady, casting long, trembling shadows. No hand is seen.

text: Not much. Just a roll. Like someone had brushed it with a sleeve.
picture: Close on June's face. It's lit only by the cold blue glow of her phone screen. Her eyes are wide, staring fixedly at the phone, refusing to look down. Her jaw is tight with dread.

text: I didn't look at the book. I looked at the camera. On the screen, I was sitting at the desk.
picture: June's phone screen in a low-angle shot. On the screen is a grainy black-and-white security feed view. It shows the back of June's head as she sits at the desk. The rest of the dim office stretches out behind her.

text: And behind me, close enough to breathe on my neck, a
picture: A close shot from behind June's shoulder. On her phone screen, the grainy CCTV image shows the back of her head and, directly behind her, the top of a tall, thin, hooded figure in a dark, dripping raincoat.

text: man in a wet raincoat was leaning over my shoulder to write.
picture: A wide 'CCTV' view from the high corner of the office. June sits at the desk. Directly behind her, the tall, skeletal figure in the dripping dark raincoat bends over her shoulder, its hooded face aimed down at the guest book, one pale hand reaching for the pen.

text: I didn't turn around. I couldn't.
picture: An extreme close-up on June's face from the front, frozen. Her eyes are wide with raw terror, glistening with unshed tears, staring straight ahead. A single drop of water falls from above, tracing a cold line down her cheek.

text: When the lights came back, the office was empty.
picture: The empty motel office from the doorway. The counter and open guest book in wet-looking light. No one is there.

text: The book was open. The ink was still wet.
picture: Close-up on the guest book. A fresh line in wet, glistening red ink: 'June Marsh, Room 6'. A puddle of water beads the counter beside it.

text: Room six. Two fourteen a.m. And the name was mine.
picture: June's hand trembles as her fingertip almost touches the wet red ink of her own name in the book. Her face, pale with terror, reflected dimly in the puddle on the counter.

text: Mr. Pell came in at six. He read the line very quietly.
picture: Mr. Pell stands behind the counter, reading glasses on, his kind, sad face lit by a desk lamp as he stares at the guest book with the red entry.

text: Then he took a key off the hook. A key I had never seen.
picture: Mr. Pell's aged hand takes an old brass key on a faded red tag from a shadowy pegboard hook behind the counter.

text: "It's always the one at the desk," he said. "Your room's ready."
picture: Mr. Pell holds the brass key out across the counter towards June, who is a blurred figure in the foreground. His expression is deeply sorrowful.

text: The Wayside Motel is still open. The night desk is always staffed. And if you sign the book, check the name above yours.
picture: In the Hollow, the Storyteller lowers his glowing red lantern. Far behind him in heavy fog, a dark row of motel doors. One door is boarded but stands open, a dim light within.
